The power went out in the co-working space ten minutes before Vandana's pitch, and her laptop battery showed four percent.

She had one chance with Anirban, an angel investor who had flown in for the day. No slides now. She pulled out the printed order sheets from her millet-snack stall: 312 customers in six months, 140 of them buying again.

"I started with a stall outside a school," she said, holding up a packet. "Parents asked for less sugar, so I changed the recipe twice."

Anirban read the sheets by his phone torch. "Why haven't shops picked you up?"

"Two tried. I couldn't keep up with packaging."

He didn't invest. But he said, "Your repeat numbers are real. Fix supply, then call me."

Walking home in the rain, Vandana was disappointed and oddly light. She wrote "supply first" on her wrist in pen.

qa.a: 140 of the 312 customers were buying again.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel after Anirban declined to invest?
qa.a: Vandana was disappointed, but also oddly light, because his feedback told her exactly what to fix next.

qa.a: She could sort out packaging and supply so shops can stock her snacks, then go back to Anirban with those results.

qa.a: Anirban was impressed by her real customer numbers and her calm under pressure, even if the business was not ready for his money yet.

Suraj pinned the last invoice to the corkboard in their tiny office above a Pune sweet shop and sat down heavily.

Eighteen months ago, he and Tushar had started a doorstep bicycle-repair service. Students loved it. The trouble was that students also moved away every summer, and the mechanics cost more than the bookings brought in.

"We shut it on the 30th," Tushar said quietly. "We agreed."

"I know." Suraj stared at the board. "I keep thinking if we'd just raised money in March..."

"We'd have lost someone else's money too."

That evening, instead of drinking chai in silence, they opened a shared document titled "What we'd do differently." Tushar typed: talk to fifty customers before building anything. Suraj added: check who stays in the city. They wrote for two hours.

Before leaving, Suraj rang each of their four mechanics himself, thanking them and offering references.

qa.q: What kind of service did Suraj and Tushar start?
qa.a: They started a doorstep bicycle-repair service.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling as he stared at the corkboard?
qa.a: Suraj felt heavy with regret and disappointment, still wondering whether raising money in March could have saved the business.

qa.q: Which choice after the shutdown was wise, and why?
qa.a: Writing down what they would do differently turned the failure into lessons, and calling the mechanics kept trust and respect intact.

qa.q: How might the four mechanics feel about the shutdown?
qa.a: They would be worried about losing work, but Suraj's personal call and offer of references would help them feel respected rather than dropped.

grounding: Two young founders close a venture that did not work, reflect on why, and learn from the shutdown while treating their workers fairly.

12 March

The agency sent the new rates today. Translation work is now "post-editing", fixing what the machine writes, at a third of the old pay. Half my regular clients have gone quiet.

I sat by the window for an hour feeling like a typewriter in a museum.

Called Anirban, who ran the Marathi desk before I did. He said, "Dhruv, the machine can't tell if a pharmacy leaflet sounds scary to a grandmother. You can." He's moved into localisation testing, checking whether apps actually make sense to real users in each language.

So, a plan. Not a panic.
1. The six-week evening course in localisation testing Anirban mentioned. Enrol this week.
2. Keep two days for the post-editing work so rent is covered while I learn.
3. Build three sample reports on local apps and show them to Anirban by May.

Still scared. But at least I'm scared with a list.

qa.a: Translation work is now called "post-editing", fixing what the machine writes.

qa.a: Anirban likely feels sympathetic and hopeful, seeing that Dhruv's language judgement is still valuable in a new role.

For fifteen years, the typists sat under the neem tree outside the tehsil office in Samrala, and for the last three, Baljeet had sat among them with his grey machine. Now the land forms were online, and most mornings he typed nothing at all.

His niece Gurleen, home from college, found him oiling the machine for the second time that week. "Chachu, you know the forms better than anyone," she said. "People still don't know how to fill them online."

That night she showed him the government's free course for village computer centre operators. He struggled with the mouse. He felt foolish at twenty-six, learning from a girl of nineteen.

By Baisakhi, he had his certificate. He rented a corner of the photocopy shop, with a second-hand computer and a sign in Punjabi. The first customer was an old farmer from his own village, who said, "Good. Now someone will explain it properly."

passage:
Thursday night

Karthik wants the investor deck to say "82,000 active users". I ran the numbers. 82,000 people signed up. 19,000 used the app more than once last month. "Active" means the second number. He knows that.

In the meeting he said, "Everyone rounds up, Zubin. We need this round." I didn't argue in front of the others. My face was hot and I just nodded, which I hate.

I've been walking around the flat for an hour.

Here's what I'm going to do. Tomorrow morning, before the deck goes out, I'll send Karthik a short email with both numbers, the exact definitions, and a line saying I can't put my name on "82,000 active". I'll offer a better story instead: the 19,000 are growing 15 percent a month. That's actually good.

If he still wants it, I'll take it to the co-founder.

Scared of losing this job. More scared of lying to people who give us money.

qa.q: How many people used the app more than once last month?
qa.a: 19,000 used the app more than once last month.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling after nodding in the meeting?
qa.a: Zubin felt ashamed and anxious about going along silently, torn between fear of losing the job and fear of misleading investors.

qa.q: What makes Zubin's plan for the morning a wise one?
qa.a: Zubin puts both numbers and definitions in writing, refuses to sign off the false one, offers an honest positive story, and knows who to go to next.

qa.q: How might the investors be affected if the deck said "82,000 active users"?
qa.a: They would make decisions based on a misleading number and could feel betrayed later, damaging trust in the whole company.

grounding: A young analyst plans to report user numbers honestly and in writing when a manager pressures the team to inflate a metric.

The pathology lab on Station Road in Kottayam opens at seven, and Francis is usually alone at the front desk until eight.

On Tuesday a man in a white kurta came in, smiling, and leaned on the counter. "I'm from the ward councillor's office. Just tell me if Thomas from the bakery's sugar test came back high. He's standing in the co-operative election. People have a right to know."

Francis felt his neck go warm. The man was friendly, and the councillor's office paid for the lab's new signboard. "I'm sorry, I can't share anyone's reports," Francis said. "Only the patient or someone with his written permission."

"Just a yes or no."

"Not even that."

The man left without smiling. Francis wrote down the time and what was asked, and when Kavitha, the lab owner, arrived, he told her everything. She read the note, then locked the report cabinet and said, "Good. We'll write to the councillor ourselves."

qa.q: What steps did Francis take that protected the patient?
qa.a: He refused to share even a yes or no, wrote down the time and request, and reported it to Kavitha the same morning.

The pre-marriage workshop at the community hall had one strange exercise: each partner got a sheet with twenty household jobs and had to write who they imagined doing each one.

Deepika filled hers in quickly. Vishal took longer. When the facilitator asked them to swap, Deepika laughed, then stopped.

On Vishal's sheet, she had cooking, cleaning, his parents' medicines and "managing the maid". He had taken bills and the car.

"You've given me the whole house," she said quietly.

Vishal went red. "I didn't think. That's just how it is at my parents' place."

"I'll be working the same hours as you."

He looked at the list again. "Okay. What if we each take cooking three days a week? And medicines, that's my parents, so it's mine."

They spent the rest of the session crossing out and rewriting. By the end, both sheets were messy, and Deepika was smiling again.

qa.a: Each sheet had twenty household jobs.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she saw Vishal's sheet?
qa.a: Deepika felt hurt and taken aback, seeing that he imagined her doing almost all the housework though she would work the same hours.

qa.q: How did the couple handle the mismatch well?
qa.a: They named the difference openly, Vishal admitted it came from his parents' home, and they rewrote the list together into a fairer split.

Dear Zeenat,

I'm writing this instead of saying it, because every time we talk about money at dinner, one of us ends up clearing plates very loudly.

Here is what I think I understand. You want to keep sending something to your parents every month, because your father's pension is small. I grew up in a house where everything went into one account and my father decided. I don't want that for us, either.

I was hurt last week when you said I "count every rupee". I'm scared of us being careless, not of your parents.

Can we sit down on Sunday, with tea, not at dinner? Each of us writes what matters most: your parents, my savings goal, the flat. Then we work out a shared plan together, and if we get stuck, we see someone qualified who can help couples plan.

I love the life we're building. I want us to build it on purpose.

Hrithik

passage:
Sunday

Asif asked again at breakfast: "So, next year? Baby?" He was smiling.

I said, "Let's talk properly first," and he looked a bit wounded.

So I wrote the list I'd been carrying in my head.
— Work: I'm up for promotion in June. Would I still want it with a newborn? Would he step back if I did?
— Care: when Asif says he'll "help", I get tense. I don't want help. I want half.
— Money: do we know what the first year actually costs? We've never sat down with it.
— Values: how would we handle discipline? His family shouts; mine goes silent. Neither feels great.
— Us: are we ready to be tired together without blaming each other?

Tonight I showed him. He was quiet for a long time, then said, "I didn't know 'help' sounded like that." He added one line to the list himself: "Ask my brother what he wishes he'd planned."

I think we're closer to ready than we were this morning. Not there yet.

— Preeti

qa.a: Preeti is up for promotion in June.

qa.q: Why does Preeti get tense when Asif says he will "help"?
qa.a: Preeti feels uneasy because "help" suggests the care will mainly fall on Preeti, when the wish is to share it equally.

qa.q: What makes Preeti's list a useful way to decide about readiness?
qa.a: It puts work, care, money, values and the relationship on paper so the couple can talk about each one honestly instead of guessing.

qa.q: How did Asif react to seeing the list?
qa.a: Asif was quiet for a long time, surprised at how "help" sounded, and then took part by adding his own question to the list.

grounding: A young adult reflects on readiness for parenthood, listing work, care, money and values, and discusses sharing care equally with a partner.

Thursday, Darjeeling

Ama-la had a good morning. She remembered the neighbour's name and asked for her tea with extra salt, the old way. I logged into work at nine from the kitchen table so I could hear her if she called.

Afternoon was harder. She thought I was my mother and kept asking when Papa was coming home. I had a client call. I muted myself twice to answer her gently. By six my shoulders were up by my ears.

Video call with Indu in Dubai tonight. I finally said it: "I can't do all of this alone and keep my job." She went quiet, then said, "What can I take from here?"

We decided: Indu manages her medicine orders and the doctor's appointments online. She'll also pay for a helper three mornings a week, and I'll handle the rest of the bills. Saying it out loud was the hardest part.

Tenzin

Every Sunday for two years, Lucia's mother had arrived at their flat in Porto at eleven, unannounced, with a pot of soup and a list of things she had noticed were dusty.

Gabriel liked her. That was the difficult part. But after a week of night shifts at the hospital, Sundays were his only sleep.

He talked to Lucia first. "I don't want her to stop coming. I just need notice, and maybe not every week."

Lucia sighed. "You know how she is."

"Then can we tell her together?"

They invited her for lunch on a Saturday. Gabriel said, "We love your visits. But I'm sleeping on Sunday mornings after night shifts. Could you come on alternate Saturdays, and text first?"

Her face tightened. "So I'm a nuisance."

"No. You're family, and I want to be awake for you."

She left early that day. Two weeks later, a text arrived: Saturday OK? Soup.

qa.q: What did Lucia's mother bring every Sunday?
qa.a: She brought a pot of soup and a list of things she had noticed were dusty.

qa.q: What was Lucia's mother feeling when she said, "So I'm a nuisance"?
qa.a: She felt hurt and rejected, hearing the request as a sign that she was not wanted.

qa.q: What did Gabriel's approach get right in setting the boundary?
qa.a: He spoke to Lucia first, asked together with her, gave a real reason, and offered another time instead of just saying no.

qa.q: How might Lucia feel caught between her mother and Gabriel?
qa.a: Lucia may feel torn and a bit anxious, loving her mother's visits but also understanding Gabriel's need for sleep.

grounding: A young husband sets a respectful boundary with his mother-in-law's unannounced visits, together with his wife and without cutting her off.

The staffroom bell had just rung for the lunch break when the peon put his head in. "Jaya ma'am, your aunty is at the gate."

Uma Masi was there with a folder of photographs. "Only five minutes, beta. This boy is an engineer in Pune."

Jaya felt thirty pairs of eyes behind her through the staffroom window. Her hands went cold.

"Masi, come, let's walk to the tea stall," she said, steering her away from the gate. Then, quietly: "I know you're doing this because you care. But school is my workplace. I can't talk about marriage here."

"When, then? You never pick up the phone."

That was fair. Jaya took a breath. "Sunday, at your house. I'll come for lunch, and I'll look at the photos. And I'll tell you honestly what I think."

Uma Masi looked hurt, then nodded. "Sunday. And bring the halwa you make."

Jaya walked back to class twelve minutes late, shaky but relieved.

qa.q: Where did Jaya take Uma Masi to talk?
qa.a: Jaya steered her away from the gate to walk to the tea stall.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel when Uma Masi appeared at school?
qa.a: Jaya felt embarrassed and anxious, with cold hands, feeling her colleagues watching through the window.

qa.q: How did Jaya hold the boundary while keeping respect?
qa.a: She moved the talk away from the gate, named Masi's care, stated clearly that school was not the place, and offered a specific time on Sunday.

qa.q: How might Uma Masi see Jaya's request?
qa.a: Uma Masi felt hurt at first, since Jaya rarely picks up the phone, but the offer of Sunday lunch showed Jaya still wanted to talk.

grounding: A young teacher holds a boundary with her aunt about discussing marriage at her workplace, while offering respect and another time.

Subject: About the phone calls

Dear Irawati Atya,

I hope your knee is better and that the mango tree gave you a good crop this year.

I'm writing because I find it hard to say this on the phone, and I don't want to say it badly. Over the last few months, most of our calls have been about when I will get married and why I left the bank for a job at a small design studio. I know you ask because you care about me, and you've always been the one who remembered my exams and birthdays.

But these calls leave me feeling like a disappointment, and I've started dreading them. I don't want to dread talking to you.

So I'd like to ask: can we leave marriage and my job out of our calls for a while? I'll tell you when there's news, I promise. I would love to hear about your garden, and your book club, and how Ajji is.

With love and respect,
Vaibhav

qa.q: Where does Vaibhav work now?
qa.a: Vaibhav left the bank for a job at a small design studio.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling after the recent calls with Irawati Atya?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt like a disappointment and had started dreading the calls, which was sad because Vaibhav values Irawati Atya.

qa.q: What makes Vaibhav's email a respectful way to set a boundary?
qa.a: It opens warmly, acknowledges Atya's care, explains Vaibhav's feelings, makes one clear request, and offers other topics to talk about.

qa.q: How might Irawati Atya feel after reading the email?
qa.a: Irawati Atya might feel hurt or surprised at first, but also touched by Vaibhav's warmth and promise to share news, which could make it easier to agree.

grounding: A young adult writes to an aunt to set a respectful limit on questions about marriage and career while keeping their close bond.

Come, Vandana, sit. You say you have no friends in this new city and your office people are just "office people". Let your Ankita Mami tell you something.

When I was twenty-four and newly posted to Pune, I knew nobody. I went to work, came home, ate alone. The loneliness sat on me like a wet blanket.

One Sunday I saw a notice in the lift: a small library in the society office, run by volunteers. I went only because it was raining. An old professor, Mr. Kale, was sorting books. I offered to help. Then I kept going, every Sunday.

Within a year, that library had given me three friends, a mentor who helped me with my first promotion, and the family who drove me to the hospital when I fell ill.

It didn't happen at once. It happened because I kept turning up on Sundays. Pick one thing, Vandana, and keep turning up.

qa.q: Where was the small library Ankita found?
qa.a: It was in the society office, run by volunteers.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel when she first arrived in Pune?
qa.a: Ankita felt very lonely, as if the loneliness sat on her like a wet blanket.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Ankita's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Offering to help Mr. Kale and then going back every Sunday mattered, because steady presence slowly built trust and friendships.

qa.q: How might Mr. Kale have seen the young Ankita who kept coming on Sundays?
qa.a: Mr. Kale likely came to see her as reliable and grew fond of her, which is why he became a mentor who helped her grow.

grounding: An aunt tells how, at twenty-four in a new city, she built trusted friends and a mentor by regularly volunteering at a society library.

Indu had moved to Hyderabad for a hospital job with rotating night shifts, and after three months she knew exactly one person outside work: the man who sold idlis near her gate.

The shifts made everything harder. The book club met on Thursday evenings, which she usually worked. The residents' group planned outings for Sunday mornings, when she was asleep.

So she chose smaller things. She joined the building's group chat and answered questions about fevers with "please check with a doctor" and a kind word. She fixed a standing Saturday lunch with Simran, a nurse from her ward, and turned up every time, even when tired. When the elderly couple on the second floor needed someone to collect a parcel, she did it on her way back from a shift.

In the fourth month, she got flu. By noon there was khichdi from the second floor, a message from the idli man, and Simran at the door with soup.

qa.q: What made it hard for Indu to join the book club?
qa.a: The book club met on Thursday evenings, which she usually worked.

qa.q: How might Indu have felt when people arrived with food during her flu?
qa.a: Indu probably felt touched and comforted, seeing that her small efforts had built real support in a lonely city.

qa.q: What could someone with an unusual schedule copy from Indu?
qa.a: Choose small, regular commitments that fit the schedule, turn up reliably, and offer practical help to neighbours.

qa.q: How do the elderly couple on the second floor see Indu?
qa.a: They see her as a helpful, trustworthy neighbour, which is why they send khichdi when she is ill.

grounding: Despite night shifts, a young nurse invests in small, reliable connections that later become a trusted support network.

The Sunday football group in Salt Lake had fourteen regulars and no rules except "turn up". Dhruv, new to Kolkata for a testing job, turned up.

He wasn't good at football. So he did other things. He started bringing a crate of water bottles. He remembered that Vidya, the organiser, was studying for an exam, and asked how it went. When the youngest player needed interview tips for his first job, Dhruv spent two evenings practising with him.

After six months, Vidya asked him to help run the group's chat and the monthly fee sheet. "You're the one who notices things," she said.

In August, the flat Dhruv rented flooded overnight. He sent one message to the group, not expecting much. By eight in the morning, three of them were there with buckets, and Vidya had found him a sofa to sleep on for the week.

Dhruv stood in the wet hallway, laughing and close to tears.

qa.q: How many regulars did the Sunday football group have?
qa.a: The group had fourteen regulars.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling as he stood in the wet hallway?
qa.a: Dhruv felt overwhelmed with relief and gratitude, laughing and close to tears, because people he had quietly supported came to help.

qa.q: How did Dhruv build trust in the group even though he was not good at football?
qa.a: He showed up every Sunday, brought water, remembered people's lives and gave his time, making himself reliable and useful.

qa.q: How does Vidya see Dhruv's role in the group?
qa.a: Vidya sees him as the one who notices things, which is why she trusts him to help run the group and finds him a place to stay.

grounding: A young man new to a city builds trusted community ties through steady, small acts, which later support him in a crisis.

For three months after Papa died, I didn't cook. I lived on biscuits and delivery food and slept at odd hours. The flat felt too quiet and too full of his things at the same time.

It was Ishita who got me started again, but not with advice. She just came every Wednesday evening with vegetables and said, "Chop these with me." We made the dal he used to make. The first time, I cried into the onions and she pretended it was the onions.

After a few weeks, I started buying vegetables myself on Tuesdays, so they'd be ready. Then a morning walk, because Papa used to walk. Then back to my college friends' Sunday call, which I had been avoiding.

I also started seeing a grief counsellor once a week. It helped to say things aloud that I couldn't say to anyone who knew him.

I still miss him terribly. But I'm Parul again, most days, and not only the girl whose father died.

qa.q: What did Ishita bring every Wednesday evening?
qa.a: Ishita came with vegetables and said, "Chop these with me."

qa.q: How was Parul feeling the first time they cooked Papa's dal?
qa.a: Parul was overcome by grief and cried into the onions, missing her father deeply.

qa.q: What small steps helped Parul rebuild her routine?
qa.a: Weekly cooking with Ishita, buying vegetables herself, morning walks, returning to friends' calls and seeing a grief counsellor each helped a little at a time.

qa.q: What was it like for Ishita to cook with Parul during those weeks?
qa.a: Ishita probably felt sad and protective, choosing to stay quietly present and pretend the tears were from the onions to spare Parul embarrassment.

grounding: A young woman looks back on rebuilding routine, support and meaning after her father's death, helped by a friend and a counsellor.

Support centre note — Santosh, second meeting.

Santosh was laid off from the logistics firm six weeks ago along with forty others. At our first meeting he said he had stopped leaving the house before noon and had not told his parents in Nashik yet. He kept apologising for wasting my time.

Today was different. He had shaved and brought a printed résumé. He said that the night before, he finally called his parents, and his mother said, "Come home for a week, beta." He hasn't decided, but he said the call "took a stone off my chest."

We set a simple routine together: up by eight, two hours of job applications, one hour at the library's free course, a walk in the evening. He also joined the centre's Tuesday group for people who've lost jobs. "At least I won't be the only sad one," he joked.

I noticed his hands were steady today.

— Mohit, career support counsellor

qa.q: How many others were laid off from the logistics firm along with Santosh?
qa.a: Santosh was laid off along with forty others.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel after calling his parents?
qa.a: Santosh felt relieved, saying the call "took a stone off my chest", after carrying the secret and the shame of the job loss.

qa.q: How could Mohit keep supporting Santosh's recovery?

18 October

Six months since the last treatment. Dr. Pillai says the scans are clear, and everyone keeps saying, "Now you can go back to normal." I don't know what normal is any more.

My body tires at odd times. I used to run the office cricket team. Now I'm happy if I walk to the end of the lane without stopping.

Divyansh has been patient. He doesn't say "normal". Today he just asked, "What do you want your days to look like?" I didn't have an answer, which frightened me.

So tonight I wrote down three things I want back, slowly: my morning walk, painting on Sundays, lunch with my team once a week. Nothing about running the cricket team yet.

I also said yes to the survivors' circle at the hospital. The woman who runs it had the same treatment two years ago. I think I need people who don't need me to explain.

Vinita

qa.q: How long has it been since Vinita's last treatment?
qa.a: It has been six months since the last treatment.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling when she had no answer to Divyansh's question?
qa.a: Vinita felt frightened and lost, unsure what daily life should look like after serious illness.

qa.q: What makes Vinita's three-thing list a good way to rebuild?
qa.a: It sets small, slow goals linked to what Vinita values, and joining the survivors' circle adds support from people who understand.

qa.q: How might Divyansh see this time of Vinita's recovery?
qa.a: Divyansh seems patient and caring, perhaps worried, but choosing to ask what Vinita wants rather than pushing for a return to "normal".

It's been a year since the bus hit our auto on the highway. I walked away with stitches, and for months I told everyone I was fine.

I wasn't. Every time a horn blared, my whole body jumped. I stopped taking autos and paid for cabs I couldn't afford. I snapped at colleagues when they came up behind me. I slept with the light on.

It was my manager who noticed first. She saw me freeze at a car horn outside the office and asked, gently, if I'd talked to anyone. I said no, of course.

A month later I booked a session with a therapist, Ishita, through the company's staff support line. The first few sessions, I mostly stared at the carpet. Slowly she helped me notice what my body did, name the moments, and practise staying with them.

Last week I took an auto to the station. My hands shook. I got there anyway. I'm Farhan, and I'm learning that fine and healing are not the same thing.

qa.q: How long ago did the bus hit the auto?
qa.a: It has been a year since the bus hit the auto on the highway.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel during the auto ride to the station last week?
qa.a: Farhan was still frightened, with shaking hands, but also quietly proud to have got there anyway.

qa.q: What helped Farhan start healing, and what could help others in a similar place?
qa.a: A manager gently noticing and a therapist helping name and practise the hard moments helped; others could also reach out to trusted people and professional support.

qa.q: How might Farhan's colleagues have seen the snapping at first?
qa.a: They probably felt hurt or confused by it, not knowing that the accident still affected Farhan when people came up from behind.

grounding: A young adult recognises lingering effects of a road accident a year later and begins healing through therapy and gradual steps.

Support group note — Thursday circle.

Ritu has come to four sessions since the fire in her building in March. Tonight was the first time she spoke for more than a minute.

She said she still smells smoke that isn't there, and checks the gas knob five or six times before sleeping. She moved in with her cousin and felt guilty for "taking up space". She kept her hands under her thighs while she talked.

When she finished, another member, who lost his shop to a fire years ago, told her the smell had faded for him slowly, and that the group had helped more than he expected. Ritu cried a little and laughed at herself for crying.

I reminded her that the counsellor at the district hospital sees people from our group, and she took the number this time. She also agreed to come early next week to help set up chairs, which I think she wanted: something useful to do.

— Bhavna, group facilitator

Monday

Went back to the lane today. The one where it happened in January.

For six months I've been taking the long way home, twenty extra minutes, and telling myself it's for exercise. Tanuja knew it wasn't. She never said anything, just walked the long way with me when she could.

In therapy, Dr. Rao and I have been practising the breathing and the "five things I can see" exercise when my chest tightens. She suggested I try the lane in daylight, with someone I trust, and leave whenever I want.

So at four today, Tanuja and I walked it. My chest went tight at the corner by the tailor's shop. I stopped, named five things, a red scooter, a dog, a broken pot, a kite, Tanuja's green scarf, and kept going.

We made it to the end. I sat on the step outside the chemist and couldn't stop shaking for a bit. Tanuja bought two cold drinks and waited.

Preeti

qa.q: Where did Preeti's chest go tight?
qa.a: Her chest went tight at the corner by the tailor's shop.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel after reaching the end of the lane?
qa.a: Preeti was shaken and trembling, but likely also relieved at having faced the lane.

qa.q: Which choices made the walk safe and helpful?
qa.a: Going in daylight, with a trusted friend, using the grounding exercise from therapy, and being free to leave at any time.

qa.q: What was it like for Tanuja to walk the lane with Preeti?
qa.a: Tanuja was probably worried but steady, choosing to stay quietly present and patient rather than pushing or asking questions.

grounding: A young adult working with a therapist and a trusted friend gradually faces a place linked to a frightening experience as part of healing.
